summary.text: For the prime \(41\equiv1\pmod{20}\), the representation \(41=6^2+5\cdot1^2\) makes the relevant hypothesis hold, while the universally quantified choices \(x=0\) and \(x=1\) force the same sum to be congruent to \(-82\) and \(-78\) modulo \(41^2\). These residues differ by \(4\), which is not divisible by \(41^2\), giving a contradiction.

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
a(n)=\sum_{j\ge 0}(-4)^j\binom{n}{2j}^{2}\binom{2j}{j}^{2},
\qquad
S_p=\sum_{n=0}^{p-1}a(n).
\]
(The sum defining \(a(n)\) is finite, because \(\binom n{2j}=0\) for \(2j>n\).) Equivalently,
\[
a(n)=\sum_{j=0}^{n}(-4)^j\binom nj^2\binom{n-j}{j}^2,
\]
since
\[
\binom nj\binom{n-j}{j}
 =\frac{n!}{j!j!(n-2j)!}
 =\binom n{2j}\binom{2j}{j},
\]
and both sides vanish when \(2j>n\).

We disprove the precise proposition in the accepted statement. Its quadratic-form predicate is
\[
R(N):\Longleftrightarrow \text{there exist integers }u,v\text{ such that }N=u^2+5v^2.
\]
The first clause of the proposition says that if a prime \(p\) is congruent to \(1\) or \(9\pmod {20}\), then, for every pair of integers \(x,y\),
\[
R(p)\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
S_p\equiv 4x^2-2p\pmod {p^2}.
\tag{1}
\]
The crucial feature of (1) is that the variables \(x,y\) on the right are not the witnesses occurring in \(R(p)\). The assertion \(R(p)\) merely says that some pair \(u,v\) represents \(p\); once that existential assertion is true, (1) claims the displayed congruence for every independently chosen \(x,y\).

Take
\[
p=41.
\]
This number is prime: any proper prime divisor would be at most \(\sqrt{41}<7\), so it would have to be \(2,3\), or \(5\), but \(41\) is divisible by none of these. In particular, \(41\ne2,5\), as required by the preliminary hypotheses of the proposition. Moreover,
\[
41\equiv1\pmod {20},
\]
so the first clause applies. Finally,
\[
41=6^2+5\cdot1^2=36+5,
\]
and hence \(R(41)\) is true.

Write simply
\[
S=S_{41}=\sum_{n=0}^{40}a(n).
\]
We do not need to evaluate this integer. Because the statement quantifies over all integers \(x,y\), first choose \(x=0\) and \(y=0\). Notice that this pair need not itself represent \(41\): the antecedent in (1) is the separate existential assertion \(R(41)\), already established using \((u,v)=(6,1)\). Formula (1) therefore gives
\[
S\equiv 4\cdot0^2-2\cdot41=-82\pmod {41^2}.
\tag{2}
\]

Now choose instead \(x=1\) and \(y=0\). The very same true antecedent \(R(41)\) gives
\[
S\equiv 4\cdot1^2-2\cdot41=4-82=-78\pmod {41^2}.
\tag{3}
\]

Congruence modulo a fixed modulus is transitive, so (2) and (3) imply
\[
-82\equiv-78\pmod {41^2}.
\]
Equivalently, \(41^2\) must divide their difference
\[
(-78)-(-82)=4.
\]
But \(41^2=1681\), and \(1681\nmid4\). Indeed, a positive integer larger than \(4\) cannot divide the nonzero integer \(4\). This is a contradiction.

Thus the universally quantified proposition in the accepted statement is false, with \(p=41\) providing the counterexample. No computation of the sequence values or of \(S_{41}\) is needed: the malformed quantification forces the single integer \(S_{41}\) into two incompatible residue classes.

This argument specifically disproves the formal proposition stated above. In the usual intended reading of Sun’s conjecture, the same \(x,y\) that occur in the conclusion are required to satisfy \(p=x^2+5y^2\) (or \(2p=x^2+5y^2\) in the second case). Under that intended binding, the choices \(x=0\) and \(x=1\) made here would not be permissible representations of \(41\), so this logical counterexample does not by itself disprove that correctly bound version.
